# Results by Item {.tabset}

In this section, we examined datasets showing particularly large discrepancies between normScore and Reviewer 1 assessments to investigate the underlying causes. The ultimate goal was to identify potential limitations or systematic issues in normScore.

```{r}
# Selecting datasets with pairwise = 0 and cor = -1
df <- summaryByItem$results %>% 
  filter(pairAccuracy == 0.5 | spearman < 0 | tau < 0) %>%
  arrange(Item, pairAccuracy, spearman, tau)

DT::datatable(df, extensions = "Buttons", rownames = F, escape = F,
              options = list(ordering = T, dom = "Brt", scrollY = F,
                            scrollX = F, pageLength = nrow(df),
                            columnDefs = list(list(className = 'dt-center', targets = '_all')),
                            full_width = TRUE, rowCallback = DT::JS(js),
                            buttons = list(list(extend = "copy", text = "Copiar"),
                                          list(extend = "csv"), 
                                          list(extend = "excel")), 
                            language = list(url = "https://cdn.datatables.net/plug-ins/1.11.5/i18n/es-ES.json"))) %>% 
DT::formatStyle(1, font = 'bold') %>% DT::formatRound(3:5, digits = 2)

# table(table(df$ID)>1)
```



## Item 3 {.tabset}

Potential reasons for discrepancies:

* Disagreement between the assessment of the MA plot shape and the assessment of its alignment around y = 0. This is particularly relevant when:

    
    * The dataset contains relatively few proteins.
    * There are numerous outliers at high average expression values (X-axis).
    * Differences between normalization methods are small because all methods perform well, making it difficult for Reviewer 1 to establish a clear ranking.
    * MA plots exhibit unusual shapes.

Importantly, these discrepancies did not affect the final selection of normalization methods in any of the examined cases, as their impact was compensated for by the remaining normScore items.

Another important consideration concerns Quantile normalization, which generally performs best for Item 6 because its underlying normalization procedure directly addresses the distributional characteristics evaluated by this item. This gives Quantile normalization a certain advantage within normScore. However, since Quantile normalization is a relatively simple method that performs well across many datasets, this advantage may be beneficial in practice. Even when Quantile is not necessarily the optimal method for a particular dataset, its selection may still lead to satisfactory normalization performance.

### PXD055964 {-}

Item 3 evaluates both the alignment of proteins around y = 0 in the MA plot (logFC versus average expression) and the overall shape of the point distribution, particularly the expected decreasing wedge-shaped pattern.

In this dataset, the discrepancy between normScore and Reviewer 1 may arise because, although the MA plots generally exhibit appropriate shapes across normalization methods, some proteins show extreme values on the Y-axis across the range of average expression values. These outliers may influence the assessment of the overall MA plot shape.

Therefore, the discrepancy appears to be associated with the influence of outliers on the evaluation of both MA plot shape and alignment around y = 0.

```{r}

  mutate(Ranking = order(Ranking))
```

### PXD028841 {-}

```{r include = F}
idDataset <- "PXD028841"
bestGS <- resAllGS$globalBests[[idDataset]]
worstGS <- resAllGS$globalWorst[[idDataset]]
bestNS <- resAllNS$resGlobal[[idDataset]]
```


At the overall ranking level, rather than specifically for Item 3, this dataset shows relatively small differences between normalization methods. normScore provides a detailed ranking based on these subtle differences, whereas Reviewer 1 selected the simplest method following Occam's razor, since all normalization methods performed satisfactorily. The relatively small number of proteins in this dataset may also contribute to the difficulty of distinguishing between methods.

* normScore ranking: `r paste0(bestNS, collapse = " > ")`

* Reviewer 1 recommended methods: `r paste0(bestGS, collapse = ", ")`

* Reviewer 1 excluded methods: `r paste0(worstGS, collapse = ", ")`

In this case, particular attention should be paid to the total normScore values and their bootstrap confidence intervals. The scores are very similar across normalization methods, suggesting that their performance differences are limited and that selecting the simplest method may be a reasonable choice.

It is worth noting that normScore values can theoretically range from 0 to 7.1 for each normalization method, with lower values indicating better normalization performance and higher values indicating poorer performance (the upper limit may be higher for Log normalization).

In this dataset, the maximum observed normScore value was only 2.69, while the best-ranked normalization method (Median) obtained a score of 2.0. These relatively low values further suggest that all evaluated normalization methods performed reasonably well.

# Overall assessment

The following sections examine discrepancies between Reviewer 1's assessments and normScore at the top and bottom of the rankings.

## Top issues {.tabset}

We examined the nine cases in which the normalization method recommended by Reviewer 1 did not appear among the top three methods ranked by normScore. In most cases, all methods performed reasonably well, with only minor differences between them. Reviewer 1 generally preferred the simplest method, usually Median normalization. The small differences captured by normScore were enough to place that method outside the top three.


```{r}
dfAux <- summaryGlobal$Bests$hitRes %>% as.data.frame
dfAux$Total <- rowSums(dfAux)
colnames(dfAux) <- c("Top 1", "Top 2", "Top 3", "Total")
df <- dfAux %>% arrange(Total)

DT::datatable(df, extensions = "Buttons", rownames = T, escape = F,
              options = list(ordering = F, dom = "Brt", scrollY = '500px',
                            scrollX = F, pageLength = nrow(df),
                            columnDefs = list(list(className = 'dt-center', targets = '_all')),
                            full_width = TRUE, rowCallback = DT::JS(js),
                            buttons = list(list(extend = "copy", text = "Copiar"),
                                          list(extend = "csv"), 
                                          list(extend = "excel")), 
                            language = list(url = "https://cdn.datatables.net/plug-ins/1.11.5/i18n/es-ES.json"))
              ) %>% 
  DT::formatStyle(1, font = 'bold')

```

## Bottom issues {.tabset}

Some normalization methods that Reviewer 1 excluded nevertheless ranked near the top of the normScore ranking. The main reason was the strong correction applied by Item 0 when between-sample variability was low, which resulted in Log normalization receiving the lowest (best) overall score. Reviewer 1 excluded Log normalization because it performed poorly on one item, while its performance on the remaining items was satisfactory. 

```{r}
dfAux <- summaryGlobal$Worst$mrrResTop # %>% as.data.frame
idDataset <- names(dfAux[dfAux >= 1/3])

for (id in idDataset){
  cat("\n\n### ", id, " {-}\n\n")
  # Tabla
  gsworsts <- resAllGS$globalWorst[[id]]
  # gsworsts <- resAllGS$globalWorst[[id]]
  df <- resNS[[id]]
  df$Ranking <- 1:8
  df$GS <- c(rep("", 8-length(gsworsts)), gsworsts)
  df$NS <- rownames(df)
  df <- df %>% dplyr::select(Ranking, NS, GS, TotalCorrected, everything())

  print(htmltools::tagList(DT::datatable(df, extensions = "Buttons", rownames = F, escape = F,
                options = list(ordering = T, dom = "Bfrt", scrollY = T,
                              scrollX = T, pageLength = nrow(df),
```
